new_statements.quote: There are four possible ways of accounting for the behaviour of tone in these paradigms. Three of these involve assuming that the adjective or pronoun has one of the three Ogori tones as its underlying tone (low, mid, high).
new_statements.citation: Chumbow, Beban Sammy. 1982. Contraction and tone polarization in Ogori. Journal of West African Languages 12(1): 89-103.
new_statements.locator: p. 99 (PDF page 11); tone reduction principle p. 100, conclusion p. 101
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ogori/Òkó is described as a tone language with three level tonemes (low, mid, high) plus derived tonal glides and duplex tones that reduce by the hierarchy H > L > M; no source opened says anything about word stress or accent. Corroborated second-hand by Storch's 2013 review of Atoyebi 2010, which reports 'die drei Tonemen des Oko (hoch, mittel, tief)' and that vowel length is not significant, and by the TOC of Atoyebi 2010 whose only suprasegmental section is §3.5 'The Òko tone system'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress; Chumbow notes tonal glides surface only in deliberate (slow) speech and are reduced in normal speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Chumbow's data are cross-word-boundary (noun+adjective, possessive+noun, pronoun+verb) contraction phenomena; the three-tone statement concerns the lexical tone inventory. Nothing on citation-form vs phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Chumbow 1982 and the Ilorin theses use the name 'Ogori' (the town / Oko dialect); Atoyebi 2010 treats Oko (Ogori) and Osanyen (Magongo) as two dialects with minor phonological differences and rejects Eni as a distinct dialect; Akerejola writes Ò̩kọ/Òkó. All refer to the Oko dialect of okoe1238; no separate glottocode needed.

sources.quote: There are four possible ways of accounting for the behaviour of tone in these paradigms. Three of these involve assuming that the adjective or pronoun has one of the three Ogori tones as its underlying tone (low, mid, high).
sources.locator: p. 99 (PDF page 11); tone reduction principle p. 100, conclusion p. 101
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent (only 'prosodique' in the French abstract). Treats Ogori as a tone language with three tones (low, mid, high), tonal glides/duplex tones, tone polarization and a Tone Reduction Principle H > L > M (pp. 98-101). Scan without text layer; scanned at 300 dpi  and p. 99 checked against the page image.

sources.citation: Akerejola-Eminefo, Ernest S. 2019. A realistic orthography for Ò̩kọ. Journal of West African Languages 46(1): 73-86.
sources.note: No mention of stress or accent. Gives consonant and vowel phoneme inventories (28 phonemes) and refers to 'prosodic tones' isolated by their contribution to interpersonal meaning (p. 79); cites Akerejola 1985 (BA, ABU Zaria) as the first systematic phonology of Ogori.

sources.citation: Storch, Anne. 2013. Review of J. D. Atoyebi, A Reference Grammar of Oko. Orientalistische Literaturzeitung 108(2): 141-143. DOI 10.1524/olzg.2013.0021.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Summarises Atoyebi's ch. 3 (pp. 30-60): syllable structure, elision, assimilation, ATR vowel harmony, and 'die drei Tonemen des Oko (hoch, mittel, tief)' with grammatical tone; also 'Vokallänge ist nicht signifikant' (p. 141). Image PDF, scanned.
